sections.html:
Springfield sits at the southern end of the Willamette Valley as a separate Lane County city, and together with Eugene to the west it makes up the Eugene-Springfield metro area. Interstate 5 is the usual dividing line, and the McKenzie River forms the northern edge. Elevation is about 476 feet.

The 2020 count was 61,851 residents in 24,764 households, and 52.9 percent of occupied housing units were owner-occupied. School and utility boundaries do not always follow the city line. Some western parts of Springfield fall inside the Eugene School District 4J, so a buyer's school question can depend on the exact street.

Springfield recognizes seven neighborhood areas, and most of the city is in the Springfield School District.

  • Downtown, home to the Washburne Historic District
  • East Kelly Butte
  • East Main
  • Gateway
  • Glenwood and Glenwood Riverfront
  • Mid-Springfield
  • Q Street

The Washburne Historic District has its own rules. The city's ADU process, for one, calls for a Type 2 application there. A seller with a downtown house who expects a buyer to make changes should ask the planning desk first.

Hot, dry summers and wet, mild winters define the year. For a house, the long damp season is the main factor: roofs, gutters, crawlspaces and siding take the beating, and buyers' inspectors check them closely. The McKenzie and Willamette rivers are close, so check a parcel's flood mapping if it sits low.

sections.h2: Selling a house with an ADU
sections.html:
Springfield allows accessory dwelling units, and through June 30, 2027, subject to annual review, the city waives transportation, stormwater and local wastewater system development charges for newly permitted ADUs.

  • Willamalane Park and Recreation District charges still apply, though it allows deferral.
  • Most ADUs use a Type 1 land use application. The Washburne Historic District or alternative design standards call for Type 2.
  • A building permit follows land use approval.
  • The city offers a free ready-build ADU plan that reduces plan review fees.
  • Oregon law (House Bill 2001) bars cities from requiring ADU parking.

An ADU can be an apartment in an existing home or garage, an addition, a freestanding cottage or a conversion of an existing dwelling under 800 square feet. If you inherited a house with an unpermitted second unit, call the Planner on Duty at 541-726-3753 before listing. The city's ADU page lists the steps.

Lane County splits the bill into three installments: November 15, February 15 and May 15. A due date landing on a weekend or holiday slides to the next business day.

Payment optionDue dateDiscount
Pay in fullNovember 153%
Pay two-thirdsNovember 152% on that amount
Pay one-thirdNovember 15None

Interest on late payments is 1.333 percent a month, 16 percent over a year, beginning December 16 on the first installment, February 16 on the second and May 16 on the third. Make checks payable to the Lane County Tax Collector, or pay online by card, e-check, Google Pay or Apple Pay. Value appeals close December 31. The county payment page has details.

sections.h2: What a Springfield seller must disclose
sections.html: Each buyer who writes an offer is owed a property disclosure statement under Oregon law, and has five days after delivery to revoke. ORS 105.470 excludes personal representatives, trustees, conservators, guardians, financial institutions selling after foreclosure and government agencies, who fill out only Section 1.

The Springfield Utility Board supplies electric and water service in the city, so a buyer will transfer accounts there at closing. The council authorized a city-owned electric system by amending the charter on June 24, 1949.

Selling as-is is permitted. The Oregon disclosure statement still goes to the buyer unless an exclusion fits, and a cash buyer sets a price for the house as it stands. Set any offer beside what a listing would net once repairs, fees and carrying months are subtracted.

1. Tell the buyer the address, condition and your target closing date.
  2. Read the written offer, including closing costs and as-is wording.
  3. Escrow opens at a title company, which searches for liens and unpaid taxes.
  4. You sign, the deed is recorded and you are paid.

No lender is involved, so there is no loan appraisal to wait on.
Overdue property tax comes out of your proceeds at closing, interest included. A payoff figure from the title company, requested at the start, shows your net before you agree to anything.

• Photo ID matching the deed.
  • The latest tax statement.
  • Lender and loan number for any mortgage payoff.
  • Permit papers for any ADU or second unit.
  • Lease records if a tenant lives there.

sections.h2: If the house has an unpermitted second unit
sections.html: Inherited houses sometimes come with a converted garage or back room that was rented out without a permit. Buyers and their inspectors notice. Call the Planner on Duty at 541-726-3753 before you list and ask what the city would require to legalize the unit, or whether it is easier to sell with the unit disclosed as it stands. Because the city currently waives several development charges for newly permitted ADUs, legalizing may cost less than you expect, though Willamalane charges still apply. A cash buyer can take the property with the unit as is, which spares you the permit work.

sections.h2: Getting the house ready for showings
sections.html: Start with the parts of the house that suffer most in a damp valley: clear the gutters, check the crawlspace for moisture, and look at roof edges and siding where water sits. If the lot is low, have flood mapping information in hand. Small fixes made before an inspection often cost less than the price reduction a buyer asks for afterward. If you would rather skip the work, an as-is sale lets the buyer take on those repairs.

A title company runs the closing. Both sides sign, the deed is recorded, and your mortgage payoff, any unpaid taxes and the current tax proration come out of the price. The rest goes to you. When no lender is involved, the date can follow your moving plans instead of a bank's calendar.

Because Lane County installments fall in November, February and May, and late interest begins the day after each, it helps to close with the next installment in mind. Ask the title company how the current installment will be handled, and confirm whether the buyer or you will pay it. Settling that question in writing avoids a dispute at the signing table.

faqs.a: No. Springfield is its own city in Lane County, forming the eastern half of the Eugene-Springfield metro area. Interstate 5 mainly divides the two, though a few western Springfield areas sit in the Eugene School District 4J.

faqs.q: When are Springfield property taxes due?
faqs.a: Lane County installments are due November 15, February 15 and May 15. A full payment by November 15 earns a 3 percent discount. Late interest runs 1.333 percent a month.

faqs.q: Can I build an ADU in Springfield?
faqs.a: Yes. The city allows ADUs and, through June 30, 2027, waives transportation, stormwater and local wastewater system development charges for newly permitted units, subject to annual review.
The Springfield Utility Board provides electric and water service.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Springfield house as-is?
faqs.a: Yes. You still provide the Oregon disclosure statement unless an exclusion applies, and a cash buyer prices the house in its current condition.
